👋 About Me

Hey, I'm Austin, the actual human behind these projects. I mostly mess around with Shizuku/Dhizuku and Samsung One UI, and a lot of what I ship started as a fork of something I loved but wanted to bend a little further.

Most of it gets built and tested right on my phone, in a terminal, with AI pair-programmers (Claude, Antigravity, Codex) doing a lot of the heavy lifting. I'm not shy about that, and I still read what ships.

  • 🔧 Kotlin + Jetpack Compose is my daily driver
  • 📱 Power-user at heart: if a setting is hidden, I want to know why
  • 🧪 Some of this is hobby-project rough around the edges. I'll say so when it is.

🔭 What I'm Up To

  • ⚡ ShizukuPlus: the Plus API suite, plus keeping One UI and Android 16+ happy
  • 📦 ObtainiumPlus: better app-update management
  • 🎛️ SuperShade: my own take on the notification shade

💬 Hit a bug or have an idea? Open an issue on ShizukuPlus. I read them all, promise.

🚀 Featured Projects

**1785 ★ · 208.3k ⬇** · Kotlin

My fork of Shizuku. It pulls Root, ADB and Dhizuku into one backend, adds a Plus API on top, and smooths out One UI / Android 16+ quirks. Apps that already use Shizuku should just work.

Ciao, I'm Paolo Antinori 👋

Engineering manager at IBM, based in Italy. I grew up in the JVM and distributed-systems world and never really left; I just kept expanding the definition of "system" until it included Zigbee bulbs, travel routers, patent portals, and one robot with a Discord account. Managing engineers pays the bills; the patches below keep my hands honest.

I hold a growing pile of patents across cloud, security, automotive, developer tooling and, apparently, quantum (receipts on Google Scholar), which is the paperwork you get for writing down every "wait, that's broken" you trip over.

There is more paper behind that: Java certifications from the Sun Microsystems era, Red Hat certifications, a MongoDB course, and one about the weird parts of JavaScript. LinkedIn keeps the details.

The rest of this page is receipts.

Shipped, not just pushed

The work that means the most to me is software strangers run on their own devices:

  • Anti-Vocale (repo, F-Droid, Google Play): an Android app that transcribes voice messages entirely on-device; no internet, no subscription, any language the installed models cover. It exists because WhatsApp, Telegram and Signal each refuse this in their own way. The multilingual model zoo behind it (24 quantized ONNX ASR models, from Italian whisper to streaming Nemotron) lives on my Hugging Face, and reproducible builds ship via my fdroiddata mirror.
  • hhighlighter: a tiny shell tool to highlight terms on the command line. Still my most-starred repo, which proves the universe has strong opinions about effort versus impact.
  • jellyfin-alexa-plugin: self-hosted Alexa voice control for my Jellyfin media server (upstream by infinityofspace; mine is the patched fork, next to a patched trakt plugin).

Paying the upstream tax

Honestly, the work I'm proudest of often lives in somebody else's repository. A repo of my own is a weekend; a correct two-line patch in a compiler I depend on is a covenant. In the last two years alone that added up to hundreds of pull requests across dozens of projects that aren't mine (see them all), up and down the whole stack I stand on:

  • Compilers and compute: fixes to the OpenCL-on-Vulkan compiler google/clspv (and friends) and to the kpet/clvk loader, because my hashcat rig refused to run at full speed without them.
  • The agent stack: Hermes, the agent framework my personal fleet runs on (my patches); ccgram, the Telegram bridge those agents answer through; fail-loud contracts in mnemosyne, their memory layer; Lince, the coding environment this very workstation runs in; Backlog.md; and pqc-analyzer, a coding-agent skill that audits code for post-quantum readiness.
  • Voice: VoiceStudio, the open source local answer to ElevenLabs (my patches), fed by my OmniVoice-Studio fork; ASR fixes in k2-fsa/sherpa-onnx; a patch to kyutai's pocket-tts.
  • Fault injection and the JVM: pyteman, rule-based runtime fault injection for Python and my biggest upstream destination outside the day job (the evidence); its spiritual ancestor Byteman; scalpel and modernizer on the build side.
  • WiFi drivers and firmware: monitor-mode fixes for MediaTek radios in openwrt/mt76 and null-safety in openwrt/openwrt wifi-scripts; the LEDVANCE Smart+ bulb revision I had reverse engineered added to OpenBeken, plus behavior docs for OpenBK7231T_App.
  • Home and hardware stack: Home Assistant's Thread border router, ha-smartthinq-sensors, zigbee2mqtt docs, SmartIR, custom-components/places, a bluetooth-audio watchdog, jellyfin itself, and zmk keyboard firmware.
  • Email plumbing: opt-in IMAP FROM/TO/CC search in mguessan/davmail, so local search of an Exchange mailbox stops being a lie.
  • Day job: most of the volume lands in Apicurio Registry, the open source API and schema registry I work on (my patches).

The long tail is the point: buildah, litellm, llama-bro, voxtype, places, a GNOME timezone extension, a bluetooth-audio watchdog, and more. If I use your software weekly, you have probably seen my name in your inbox. I consider that a feature, not a bug.

The hacker

I'm at my happiest inside something that was never meant to be opened.

  • osram-lightify-fw-re: OSRAM Lightify bulbs read in assembly until they gave up their power-on logic and their proprietary 0xFC0F cluster.
  • ts0505a-ota-investigation: custom OTA firmware for a budget Lidl light. Two verified candidates, both rejected with INVALID_IMAGE; the repo is the byte-level autopsy. Negative results are results.
  • opencl-apple-silicon: hashcat at 95% of native Metal, inside Linux containers on Apple Silicon, via libkrun, clvk and the clspv fixes above.
  • cookies-extractor: a minimal Android WebView app. Log in by hand, hand me the session cookies.

The fiddler

My house runs on a slow compromise between me and the cloud, and I keep winning a little more each year. A fablab membership feeds the hardware habit.

  • local_smarthinq1 (+ the HAOS addon): a fake cloud for LG ThinQ1 appliances, so they stop reporting to a datacenter.
  • ha_alexa_proactive, ha-alexa-actions-smapi and alexa-proactive-events: three takes on making the Echo's yellow ring mean something.
  • ha-google-travel-time-enhanced: Google Maps travel time with waypoint support.
  • udp-broadcast-relay-redux-openwrt: an OpenWrt package relaying UDP broadcast and multicast across VLANs without lying about the source address.
  • school-timetable-timefold-case-study: a real school timetable solved with Timefold constraint optimization on Quarkus, written up as a case study in agent-assisted development, with two solver fixes sent upstream to Timefold along the way.
  • cyberwave-trim-deployment: Ansible that keeps my patrol robot's steering trim persistent. The robot itself has a personality module and a Discord channel; one day it will also have a public repo.
  • More Home Assistant where that came from: the ha-filtered list of my repos.

The dev

Distributed systems, build tooling, API infrastructure: the unglamorous layers are where I live.

  • maven-dependency-history: why is this dependency in the output? Point it at a local checkout, get a cited-evidence answer.
  • quarkus-extension-analyzer: dependency-usage analysis that understands Quarkus build-time extension wiring.
  • maven-ci-playbook: assess before you optimize; a field-tested playbook for Maven CI with measurement tools.
  • apicurio-browser-extension: detects and renders OpenAPI specs with the Apicurio editor, straight on GitHub and GitLab.
  • gh-issue-landscape: point it at any repo's issues, get a semantic 2D topic map back.

How all of this gets built

I don't just use coding agents; I run them like an ops problem. They live on two machines bridged by a VPN as a Hermes fleet, answer to me from a terminal multiplexer and from Telegram, and take every request through a local model router whose fallback chain ends on hardware I own. When a provider starts returning empty 200s, a watchdog of mine reclassifies them as the outage they are. backlog-workbench is the public corner of that rig.

They also live under house rules, enforced by hooks rather than vibes:

  • Evidence before assertion: nothing is done until the proving command ran and somebody read the output.
  • Check the real artifact, not a proxy: the signature, the file, the tool. Version strings lie.
  • An adjacent probe proves nothing; test the exact path that failed.
  • Two failed fixes of the same kind means stop patching and go read the source.

Anti-Vocale, up top, is built this way end to end: agent-assisted, human-owned.
